title: must, have to, should: rules and advice
tagline: Rules, prohibitions and advice — and the two words that look alike but mean opposite things.
why: School rules, exam rules, health advice — must, have to and should are how English gives instructions and opinions. Reading Part 1 is full of signs that use must, mustn't and don't have to, and the exam itself has its own rules (you must bring a pencil; you mustn't use a phone). Confusing mustn't with don't have to is the single biggest trap in this area.

hook.text: Before the test, Miss Vega says: "You must bring a pencil. You mustn't talk during the test. You don't have to finish early — you can use all the time." "Should we bring a calculator?" asks Sofia. "You don't need one," says Miss Vega.
hook.ask: Must, mustn't and don't have to look similar but they mean very different things. Can you find all three and say what each one really means?

diagrams.title: How strong is the rule?

items.label: don't have to / don't need to

diagrams.caption: Should is an opinion; have to/must is a rule; mustn't is a rule that forbids.

diagrams.title: Build the sentence with must, have to, should
diagrams.caption: Mustn't = it's forbidden. Don't have to = it's not necessary, but you can if you want. They look similar — they are opposites.

diagrams.title: Rules and advice, at school and beyond

branches.label: Strong rule (now)
items: have to — a rule from outside

use.point: must and have to — strong obligation

examples.text: You must bring a pencil to the exam.
We have to wear a uniform at school.
examples.note: have to = a rule from outside (the school)

examples.text: I have to finish this project by Friday.
examples.note: have to for a fact or rule, not just an opinion

use.point: mustn't vs don't have to — the big difference

examples.text: You mustn't use your phone during the test.

examples.note: don't have to = not necessary, but you can if you want

examples.text: We don't need to bring a calculator.
examples.note: don't need to = the same meaning as don't have to

use.point: had to — obligation in the past

examples.text: Last year, we had to wear a different uniform.
examples.note: had to = the past of have to and must

examples.text: I didn't have to do homework yesterday — no classes!
examples.note: didn't have to = wasn't necessary, in the past

examples.text: Did you have to study a lot for the last test?

watch_out.wrong: You mustn't finish early — you can if you want.
watch_out.why: Mustn't means forbidden; don't have to means not necessary — they are opposites.

watch_out.wrong: We must to wear a uniform.
watch_out.why: Have to (and must) go straight before the base verb — no to.
Must never adds -s, even for he/she/it.

watch_out.wrong: Yesterday, I must study a lot.
watch_out.right: Yesterday, I had to study a lot.
watch_out.why: Must has no past form — use had to for the past.

watch_out.wrong: You should to ask the teacher.
watch_out.why: Should goes straight before the base verb, like must — no to.

l1.why: Spanish 'no tienes que' means it's not necessary — in English that's don't have to, not mustn't (which means forbidden).
The Spanish pattern 'deber + infinitivo' tempts you to add to — English have to/must never takes to.
Should is already the whole modal — don't add would or another helper before it.

l1.wrong: I must studied a lot yesterday.
l1.right: I had to study a lot yesterday.
l1.why: Must has no past tense — the past of must/have to is always had to.

remember.trick: must/have to = rule, should = advice, mustn't = forbidden!
remember.tip: Remember the opposite pair: mustn't (you can't) and don't have to (you don't need to, but you can).

lines.text: Listen carefully. You must bring a pencil and a rubber.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega

lines.text: What happens if we finish early?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega

can_do: I can talk about rules with must and have to.
I can tell the difference between mustn't (forbidden) and don't have to (not necessary).
I can give advice with should/shouldn't and talk about past obligation with had to.
summary: Must and have to = a strong rule — you have no choice.
Mustn't = forbidden (you can't). Don't have to = not necessary (you can, but you don't need to). They are opposites, not the same.
Must has no past form — for the past, always use had to / didn't have to.
All of these modals go straight before the base verb — no to, and no -s.
